questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stores the carbon in living tissue?
options: Combustion of coal, oil and natural gas
Weathering of exposed silicate rock surfaces
Photosynthesis in plants, algae and cyanobacteria
Cellular respiration in plants and animals
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose, so atmospheric carbon becomes part of the biosphere. Respiration is the tempting opposite — it breaks glucose down and releases carbon dioxide back to the atmosphere, so it is a source, not a sink. Weathering does draw carbon down, but into dissolved ions and rock, not into living tissue. Cue: if the question says 'stored in living tissue', the answer is photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which list correctly names the four interrelated Earth systems through which carbon cycles?
options: Stratosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, magnetosphere
Atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere, troposphere
Atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere
Atmosphere, ozone layer, oceans, ecosystems
questions.explanation: The four systems are the atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things), hydrosphere (water) and lithosphere (rock and soil), and carbon moves between all four. The list containing the ozone layer and oceans is tempting because those are real features, but they are parts of the atmosphere and hydrosphere, not separate systems in this model. The magnetosphere and troposphere are also not carbon reservoirs in this framework. Cue: 'lithosphere' must appear, because rock holds the largest carbon store.

questions.stem: A volcano erupts and releases gas. In terms of the carbon cycle, this transfers carbon from the:
options: atmosphere to the lithosphere
biosphere to the hydrosphere
hydrosphere to the biosphere
lithosphere to the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Vulcanism brings carbon that was locked in rock and magma deep underground to the surface, releasing carbon dioxide gas into the air. The reversed option, atmosphere to lithosphere, describes the long-term burial of carbon through weathering and sediment formation, not an eruption. Cue: gas coming out of the ground always means rock store to air store.

questions.stem: During respiration in a kangaroo, how is carbon transferred between Earth's systems?
options: From the atmosphere to the biosphere, stored as glucose in tissue
From the lithosphere to the biosphere, absorbed by digesting minerals
From the hydrosphere to the biosphere, taken in as dissolved carbonate
From the biosphere to the atmosphere, released as carbon dioxide gas
questions.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose (carbon held in living tissue, part of the biosphere) and releases carbon dioxide into the air, so carbon moves biosphere to atmosphere. The option saying carbon moves from atmosphere to biosphere as glucose describes photosynthesis, which is the reverse process, not respiration. The cue is the direction of the gas: if CO2 is being breathed out, carbon is entering the atmosphere.

questions.stem: A power station burns coal formed from plants buried 300 million years ago. Which transfer is correct?
options: Carbon in the lithosphere is converted into new fossil fuel in the biosphere
Carbon stored in the lithosphere is released into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide
Carbon in the atmosphere is transferred into the lithosphere as coal ash
Carbon in the biosphere is transferred into the hydrosphere as soot
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels are long-term carbon stores locked in rock, which is part of the lithosphere; combustion oxidises that carbon and releases it as CO2 into the atmosphere. The option about carbon moving into the lithosphere as ash reverses the transfer — burning is a release, not a burial. Ask yourself where the carbon was before and where it ends up: buried rock to air.

questions.stem: Which pair of carbon cycle processes operates mainly over millions of years rather than over days to decades?
options: Photosynthesis and respiration
Fire and photosynthesis
Respiration and combustion of fossil fuels
Weathering of rock and vulcanism
questions.explanation: Weathering slowly draws carbon out of the atmosphere into sediments, and vulcanism slowly returns it, so together they form the slow (geological) part of the carbon cycle. Photosynthesis and respiration are tempting because they are the best-known pair, but they exchange carbon over hours, days and seasons — that is the fast carbon cycle. The cue is whether rock is involved: rock processes are slow.

questions.stem: As atmospheric carbon dioxide levels rise, more CO2 dissolves in the ocean. What effect does this have on seawater?
options: It forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH of seawater
It forms carbonic acid, raising the pH of seawater
It forms carbonates that make seawater more alkaline
It has no chemical effect because CO2 dissolves without reacting
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions and lowers ocean pH — the process called ocean acidification. The option saying carbonic acid raises pH is tempting if you mix up the pH scale: adding an acid always lowers pH, because lower pH means more hydrogen ions. This shows how a change in the atmosphere alters the hydrosphere.

questions.stem: A eucalypt forest burns in a bushfire, then regrows over the following 40 years. Why is this cycle treated differently from burning an equivalent mass of coal?
options: Forest carbon comes from the soil, so the carbon released in a bushfire returns to the lithosphere
Regrowing forest reabsorbs the released carbon, while coal adds carbon that was locked away for millions of years
Bushfires release methane rather than carbon dioxide, so they do not affect atmospheric carbon at all
Coal burns at a higher temperature, so it converts a greater proportion of its carbon into carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Forest carbon is part of the fast cycle: photosynthesis during regrowth takes back roughly the CO2 that the fire released, so there is little long-term change in atmospheric carbon. Fossil carbon has been out of circulation for hundreds of millions of years, so burning it is a one-way addition to the atmosphere. The claim about burning temperature is wrong because it is the origin of the carbon, not the flame temperature, that matters.

questions.stem: Gases become less soluble in water as the water warms. What does this imply for the ocean as global temperatures rise?
options: The ocean's dissolved CO2 is unchanged, because solubility depends only on pressure
The ocean converts the extra dissolved CO2 into oxygen, restoring the original balance
The ocean holds less dissolved CO2, so more stays in the atmosphere — a positive feedback
The ocean holds more dissolved CO2, so warming is cancelled out — a negative feedback
questions.explanation: Warmer water cannot hold as much dissolved gas, so a warming ocean takes up less CO2 and can even release some, leaving more in the atmosphere and driving further warming — a reinforcing (positive) feedback. The negative-feedback option gets the solubility rule backwards: heating a fizzy drink drives gas out, it does not dissolve more. Pressure does affect solubility too, but it does not remove the temperature effect.

questions.stem: Over hundreds of millions of years, burial of dead marine organisms and their shells built up thick limestone and shale layers. What is the significance of this for Earth's systems?
options: Carbon was transferred from the lithosphere into the atmosphere, warming the early Earth
Carbon was destroyed as organisms decayed, permanently removing it from the carbon cycle
Carbon was transferred from the biosphere into the atmosphere, since burial prevents respiration
Carbon was transferred from the atmosphere and hydrosphere into long-term lithosphere storage
questions.explanation: Marine organisms build tissue and shells using carbon that came from dissolved CO2 in seawater, which in turn came from the atmosphere; burial locks that carbon into rock for geological timescales. The option about carbon being destroyed breaks conservation of matter — carbon atoms are cycled, never destroyed. Burial is the main reason atmospheric CO2 fell over Earth's history, and it explains why fossil fuel burning matters.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches a process to the direction it moves carbon?
options: Volcanism moves carbon from the atmosphere to the lithosphere
Combustion of petrol moves carbon from the lithosphere to the atmosphere
Photosynthesis moves carbon from the biosphere to the atmosphere
Respiration moves carbon from the atmosphere to the biosphere
questions.explanation: Petrol is refined from crude oil stored underground, so burning it takes carbon that was in the lithosphere and releases it as CO2 into the atmosphere. The reversed pairs are the trap: photosynthesis takes carbon in from the atmosphere while respiration gives it back, and volcanism vents carbon out of the lithosphere. Cue: check whether the process consumes CO2 or produces it before deciding the direction.

questions.stem: Marine phytoplankton in the Southern Ocean carry out photosynthesis in surface waters. Which Earth systems are directly involved in this carbon transfer?
options: Atmosphere and lithosphere, as air-borne carbon dioxide is deposited on the sea floor
Atmosphere and biosphere only, since photosynthesis always draws gas straight from the air
Hydrosphere and lithosphere, as seawater carbon is turned into sediment by the plankton
Hydrosphere and biosphere, as dissolved carbon in seawater becomes plankton tissue
questions.explanation: Phytoplankton live in seawater and use carbon dioxide dissolved in it, so the immediate transfer is from the hydrosphere into the biosphere. The 'atmosphere and biosphere only' option is tempting because photosynthesis on land does draw CO2 from air, but in the ocean the gas must first dissolve, making the hydrosphere the direct source. Cue: identify where the carbon physically sits at the moment of the transfer.

questions.stem: Warming causes Arctic permafrost to thaw, allowing microbes to decompose organic matter that has been frozen for thousands of years. Why is this described as a positive feedback?
options: The released gases reflect incoming sunlight, so the warming eventually corrects itself
The decomposition releases carbon dioxide and methane, which add to warming and cause further thawing
The extra decomposition returns nutrients to soils, which is a beneficial outcome for plant growth
The thawed ground absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, which slows further warming over time
questions.explanation: A positive feedback is one where the output of a change loops back to amplify that same change; here warming releases greenhouse gases that cause more warming and more thawing. The 'beneficial outcome' option misuses the word positive — in systems science it means self-reinforcing, not good. Cue: ask whether the effect strengthens or opposes the original change.

questions.stem: Clearing native forest for cropland changes the carbon cycle in more ways than just the loss of standing trees. Which additional effect on Earth's systems is correct?
options: Disturbed soil loses stored organic carbon to the atmosphere as decomposition speeds up
Bare soil takes up more carbon dioxide than forest did, because no leaves compete for it
Removing trees increases rainfall over the cleared area, raising the region's carbon uptake
Soil carbon is permanently locked in mineral grains, so clearing cannot affect it
questions.explanation: Soils are a major carbon reservoir, and ploughing or exposing them raises oxygen supply and temperature so microbes break down organic matter faster, sending CO2 to the atmosphere. The idea that bare soil absorbs more CO2 is wrong because soil uptake depends on plants fixing carbon in the first place; without vegetation the flow reverses. Cue: think about the whole biosphere-lithosphere link, not only the trees you can see.

questions.stem: In the carbon cycle, what does chemical weathering of rock by rainwater do?
options: Moves carbon from ocean water into the atmosphere as carbonate breaks down
Removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, carrying dissolved carbon to the oceans
Releases carbon dioxide from rock into the atmosphere, adding to volcanic emissions
Transfers carbon from the biosphere into rock as dead plant material is buried
questions.explanation: Weathering consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide: CO2 dissolved in rainwater forms a weak acid that breaks down rock, and the dissolved carbon products are carried by rivers to the ocean, where they can eventually be deposited as carbonate sediment. The tempting wrong choice is that weathering releases CO2 from rock — that describes volcanism and the heating of buried carbonate rock, not weathering. The cue is the direction: weathering is a slow atmospheric sink, vulcanism is the matching source.

questions.stem: By far the greatest amount of Earth's carbon is stored in which reservoir?
options: Coal, oil and natural gas deposits formed from ancient organisms
Carbonate rocks and sediments such as limestone in the lithosphere
Carbon dioxide and other carbon gases held in the atmosphere
Living organisms, especially forests and soils, in the biosphere
questions.explanation: Hundreds of millions of years of shell and sediment burial have locked the overwhelming majority of Earth's carbon into carbonate rocks and other sediments of the lithosphere, dwarfing every other reservoir. Fossil fuel deposits are tempting, but they are only a small fraction of lithospheric carbon — they matter because humans move them quickly, not because they are the biggest store. The atmosphere holds one of the smallest amounts, which is why relatively small transfers into it change its composition noticeably.

questions.stem: Which word equation represents cellular respiration?
options: glucose + carbon dioxide → oxygen + water, releasing stored energy
oxygen + water → glucose + carbon dioxide, using light energy
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy
questions.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and water along with usable energy, so it transfers carbon from the biosphere to the atmosphere or hydrosphere. The reversed equation with light energy is photosynthesis, the process that moves carbon the other way. Check where the light energy appears: if light is an input, the equation is photosynthesis, not respiration.

questions.stem: A healthy pot plant is sealed in a clear jar fitted with a carbon dioxide sensor and left in complete darkness for two hours. The CO2 level inside steadily rises. The best explanation is that:
options: the plant switches over to respiration in the dark, because plants only respire at night and photosynthesise by day
the plant halts all gas exchange in the dark, so the extra CO2 must be leaking in from outside the sealed jar
the plant reverses photosynthesis in the dark, breaking its stored glucose back into the carbon dioxide it came from
the plant continues respiring, but without light it cannot photosynthesise, so no CO2 is being taken back up
questions.explanation: Plants respire continuously, day and night, but photosynthesis needs light; in darkness the uptake of CO2 stops while the release continues, so CO2 in the jar accumulates. The most tempting distractor claims plants only respire at night — a very common misconception. In the light the two processes happen together and photosynthesis usually outpaces respiration, which is why a lit plant lowers CO2 rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Long-term atmospheric records show carbon dioxide rising year after year, with a small regular dip each Northern Hemisphere spring and summer. What causes the annual dip?
options: Warmer summer surface water dissolves more carbon dioxide, temporarily drawing the gas out of the atmosphere
Power stations and industry shut down over the northern summer, so fossil fuel emissions cease for several months
Summer sunlight breaks down carbon dioxide molecules in the upper atmosphere faster than they can be replaced
Vast northern land forests photosynthesise faster than decomposition and respiration release CO2 during the growing season
questions.explanation: Most of the world's land vegetation is in the Northern Hemisphere, so when it leafs out in spring the biosphere pulls CO2 from the atmosphere faster than respiration and decomposition return it, producing a seasonal dip that reverses in autumn. The claim about warmer water dissolving more CO2 is wrong in the opposite direction: gases become less soluble as water warms. The cue is that the dip tracks the northern growing season, pointing to photosynthesis in the biosphere.

questions.stem: Photosynthesis and ocean uptake still remove enormous amounts of carbon dioxide every year, yet atmospheric CO2 keeps climbing. Which explanation is correct?
options: Fossil fuel combustion returns buried carbon to the atmosphere faster than these sinks can remove it, so the surplus accumulates
Carbon dioxide made by burning fossil fuels differs chemically from natural CO2, so plants and oceans cannot absorb it
Photosynthesis has effectively ceased worldwide, so almost no carbon is now being taken out of the atmosphere at all
Carbon dioxide from combustion rises into the upper atmosphere, out of reach of plants and the ocean surface below
questions.explanation: The carbon cycle is a balance of rates: burning fossil fuels moves lithospheric carbon into the atmosphere over decades, far faster than photosynthesis, weathering and ocean uptake can transfer it back out, so the excess builds up. The idea that fossil fuel CO2 is chemically different is false — a CO2 molecule from a power station is identical to one from a bushfire, and sinks do absorb roughly half of it. Think in terms of the rate of release versus the rate of removal, not whether removal happens at all.

questions.stem: How do greenhouse gases warm Earth's surface?
options: They absorb incoming sunlight before it can reach and heat the surface
They form a reflective layer trapping warm air like a physical lid
They react with oxygen high in the atmosphere, releasing heat directly
They absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit some of it back downwards
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are largely transparent to incoming short-wavelength sunlight but absorb the longer-wavelength infrared radiation emitted by the warmed surface, re-emitting some of it back towards the ground and slowing the loss of energy to space. The option about absorbing incoming sunlight reverses the energy exchange: if that were true the surface would receive less energy and cool. The cue is the direction of the radiation — greenhouse gases act on outgoing infrared, not incoming visible light.

questions.stem: Which set of human activities are all major contributors to greenhouse gas emissions?
options: Nuclear power, reforestation, wind farms and rail electrification
Ocean acidification, ozone loss, urban noise and plastic pollution
Volcanic eruptions, solar cycles, orbital wobble and ocean currents
Fossil-fuel electricity, deforestation, cement manufacturing and transport
questions.explanation: Human-induced climate change is driven by activities that release stored carbon or produce greenhouse gases, including burning fossil fuels for power and transport, clearing forests, and industrial processes such as cement making, which releases CO2 from limestone. The list containing nuclear power and wind farms is tempting because these are energy-related, but they are low-emission options and part of mitigation, not causes. The cue is to ask whether each item adds greenhouse gases to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: As the Arctic warms, bright sea ice melts and exposes darker ocean water. What is the effect on Earth's energy balance?
options: Evaporation from the exposed water removes so much heat that regional temperatures fall
The change alters surface colour only and has no measurable effect on energy absorbed
The darker ocean absorbs more solar energy than the ice reflected, causing further warming
The darker ocean reflects more solar energy than the ice did, partly offsetting the warming
questions.explanation: Ice has a high albedo and reflects most incoming solar radiation, while open ocean is dark and absorbs it, so replacing ice with water increases the energy absorbed and drives more warming and more melting — a positive feedback. The option saying dark water reflects more reverses the relationship between colour and albedo. The cue is that dark surfaces absorb and pale surfaces reflect, the same reason a black car interior heats faster than a white one.

questions.stem: Methane makes up a much smaller share of greenhouse gas emissions than carbon dioxide, yet cutting methane is treated as a priority. Why?
options: Methane is not a greenhouse gas itself but breaks down into gases that damage the ozone layer
Methane is heavier than air, so it settles near the surface where it warms the ground directly
Methane persists in the atmosphere for many thousands of years, far longer than carbon dioxide does
Methane traps far more heat per molecule but breaks down in about a decade, so cuts slow warming quickly
questions.explanation: Methane absorbs infrared radiation much more strongly per molecule than carbon dioxide, giving it a high warming effect, but it is oxidised in the atmosphere over roughly a decade, so reducing methane emissions produces a noticeable slowing of warming within a human lifetime. The option about very long persistence is tempting because students associate potency with permanence, but methane's short lifetime is precisely why cuts act fast. The cue is to treat warming strength and atmospheric lifetime as two separate properties.

questions.stem: Which change would genuinely cut greenhouse gas emissions from a coal-fired power station?
options: Running the station only during the night, when cooler air disperses exhaust faster
Closing it and replacing its output with wind and solar feeding the same grid
Building much taller chimneys so exhaust is released high above the district
Switching from black coal to brown coal while keeping the same capacity
questions.explanation: Wind and solar generation produce electricity without burning carbon-containing fuel, so replacing coal-fired output removes the carbon dioxide released at the point of generation. Taller chimneys are tempting because they visibly improve local air quality, but they only disperse the same mass of CO2 more widely — the total emitted is unchanged. Brown coal actually releases more CO2 per unit of electricity than black coal, and shifting operation to night-time changes when gases are released, not how much.

questions.stem: Satellite measurements show that Earth is currently absorbing slightly more energy from the Sun than it radiates back to space as infrared. What does this energy imbalance indicate?
options: Greenhouse gases are absorbing incoming sunlight before it reaches the surface, which cools the surface below
Energy is accumulating in Earth's systems, mostly as heat stored in the oceans, so temperatures continue to rise
The Sun has recently increased its output, and this extra solar energy is the sole cause of the observed warming
Earth's systems are in balance overall, because the oceans return exactly as much energy as the atmosphere gains
questions.explanation: If incoming absorbed energy exceeds outgoing radiation, the surplus must be stored somewhere in the Earth system, and over 90% of it ends up as heat in the oceans, driving continued warming. The 'systems are in balance' option misreads the data — an imbalance is precisely what is measured. Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to incoming shortwave sunlight and instead absorb outgoing infrared, so they warm rather than shade the surface, and measured solar output has not risen to match recent warming.

questions.stem: A cement works powers its kiln entirely with renewable electricity, yet it still emits large amounts of carbon dioxide. What is the best explanation?
options: The high temperatures inside the kiln convert nitrogen in the air into carbon dioxide through a combustion reaction
Heating limestone chemically decomposes calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas, regardless of the heat source
Cement absorbs carbon dioxide from the air during manufacture and then releases twice as much of it during storage
Renewable electricity produces carbon dioxide directly at the kiln because it must be converted from direct to alternating current
questions.explanation: Cement production involves calcination: calcium carbonate is broken down into calcium oxide plus carbon dioxide, so the CO2 comes from the raw material itself and cannot be avoided by changing the energy source. The renewable-electricity distractor is tempting for students who assume all industrial CO2 comes from fuel burning; electrical conversion releases no carbon dioxide. Nitrogen cannot become carbon dioxide, since carbon dioxide contains carbon, and cement does not absorb CO2 during manufacture.

questions.stem: A climate model run using only natural factors (volcanic eruptions and small changes in solar output) fails to reproduce the observed warming since about 1970, but the same model matches the record closely when human greenhouse gas emissions are also included. What does this result best support?
options: The model has been deliberately adjusted, because any model can be made to match a temperature record exactly
Volcanic eruptions must be the main driver of the recent warming, since they release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
The warming since 1970 cannot be explained by natural factors alone and is consistent with human greenhouse gas emissions
Natural factors have had no influence on Earth's climate at any point during the past several thousand years
questions.explanation: This kind of paired model run is an attribution test: if the physics of natural forcings alone cannot reproduce the observations but adding human emissions does, human emissions are the necessary explanation. The 'natural factors have had no influence' option overreaches — volcanoes and solar variation do affect climate, they simply cannot account for this particular trend. Volcanic emissions of CO2 are tiny compared with fossil fuel emissions, and the fact that the natural-only run fails shows the model was not tuned to match whatever was wanted.

questions.stem: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere yet plays no direct role in the greenhouse effect?
options: Water vapour
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Methane
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases are those whose molecules absorb and re-emit infrared radiation; nitrogen (N2) is a simple two-atom molecule of identical atoms and does not do this, even though it is about 78% of the atmosphere. Water vapour is the most tempting wrong choice because students often think only 'pollution' gases trap heat, but water vapour is in fact the most abundant greenhouse gas. The cue: abundance and greenhouse activity are separate things — check whether the molecule absorbs infrared, not how much of it there is.

questions.stem: As the atmosphere warms, more water evaporates from oceans and lakes, so the air holds more water vapour. What does this do to global warming?
options: It amplifies the warming, because water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas that absorbs more outgoing infrared
It cancels the warming, because evaporation removes heat energy from the ocean surface at the same rate
It has no climate effect, because water vapour condenses back into rain within days of evaporating
It slows the warming, because extra water vapour reflects incoming sunlight straight back into space
questions.explanation: Extra water vapour absorbs more infrared radiated from the surface, causing further warming and further evaporation — a positive (amplifying) feedback triggered by the initial carbon dioxide warming. The option about water vapour condensing out quickly is tempting and half-true: individual molecules do rain out within about a week, but a warmer atmosphere maintains a permanently higher average vapour content. The cue: feedbacks are judged by the average state of the system, not by how long one molecule lasts.

questions.stem: If all human greenhouse gas emissions stopped tomorrow, global temperatures would not immediately return to pre-industrial levels. The best explanation is that:
options: greenhouse gases already emitted would keep generating new greenhouse gases through chemical reactions in the upper atmosphere
temperatures would in fact fall back within a year or two, because rainfall washes carbon dioxide out of the air very quickly
much of the added carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for centuries, and the oceans warm slowly, so the energy imbalance persists
the heat already stored in the atmosphere would take several centuries to radiate away, because air has an enormous heat capacity
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is removed only slowly by ocean uptake and weathering, so its warming influence lasts for centuries, while the deep ocean continues absorbing heat and adjusting for decades after emissions stop. The option about atmospheric heat capacity is tempting, but the atmosphere is thin and stores relatively little heat — the ocean holds the overwhelming majority of the extra energy. The cue: the lag comes from long-lived CO2 plus slow ocean heating, not from stored heat in the air.

questions.stem: Before using a climate model to project temperatures to 2100, scientists run it from 1850 to the present and compare its output with the observational record. The main scientific reason for doing this is to:
options: demonstrate that past climate was governed by different physical laws from those operating in the atmosphere today
remove the need for further temperature measurements, since a matching model replaces observations from then on
test whether the model reproduces known past changes, giving grounds for confidence in its projections of future change
confirm that the model can forecast the weather on particular past days, which is required before any long-term run
questions.explanation: A model is a simplified representation of interacting systems, and the standard way of evaluating one is to check its output against independent data it must reproduce; success over 170 years of observed change justifies some confidence in projections. The option about forecasting particular past days is tempting because it sounds like a stricter test, but climate models project long-term statistics such as decadal averages, not the weather of a given date. The cue: climate is average conditions over decades; weather is day to day.

questions.stem: A wealthy country closes its steel mills and imports the same quantity of steel from overseas instead. Its national emissions figures fall sharply. What is the best assessment of the global climate effect?
options: Global emissions are unaffected by trade in goods, because only power generation and transport are counted in global totals
Global emissions may barely change, because the manufacturing emissions have shifted to the exporting country and shipping adds more
Global emissions fall by exactly the amount the country's national figures fell, since the mills are no longer operating anywhere
Global emissions must fall further still, because steel made overseas always uses less energy per tonne than locally made steel
questions.explanation: The atmosphere responds to total global emissions, so relocating production shifts where emissions are counted (carbon leakage) without necessarily reducing them, and long-distance freight adds further fossil fuel use. The option claiming a fall equal to the national reduction is tempting because the national ledger genuinely improves, but the steel is still being made — just elsewhere. The cue: for climate outcomes, follow the emissions from consumption of goods, not the national accounting boundary.

questions.stem: Which of these actions is an example of mitigating human-induced climate change, rather than adapting to it?
options: Breeding heat-tolerant wheat varieties for hotter, drier growing seasons
Installing air conditioning in classrooms to cope with more heatwave days
Replacing a diesel bus fleet with electric buses charged from wind power
Building a higher levee bank to protect a coastal suburb from flooding
questions.explanation: Mitigation means reducing greenhouse gas emissions at their source or increasing the removal of carbon from the atmosphere; swapping diesel combustion for renewable electricity cuts emissions from transport. Building a higher levee bank is the most tempting distractor because it is clearly a climate response, but it changes nothing about emissions — it only reduces the harm from an impact that is already coming, which is adaptation. The cue: ask whether the action changes the amount of greenhouse gas entering the atmosphere (mitigation) or only how well we cope with the consequences (adaptation).

questions.stem: Why are cattle and sheep a big part of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions?
options: They exhale carbon dioxide, the largest single greenhouse gas from farming
Nitrogen in their grass becomes nitrous oxide in their lungs and is breathed out
The methane they produce stays in the atmosphere for thousands of years
Microbes in their digestive systems make methane, which they release by belching
questions.explanation: Ruminants ferment grass using gut microbes, and this enteric fermentation produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas released largely through the animals' mouths. The option about exhaled carbon dioxide is tempting because livestock certainly breathe out CO2, but that carbon came from plants that recently took it from the air, and it is methane — not respired CO2 — that makes livestock a major emissions source. Remember the key word 'enteric': the problem starts in the gut, not the lungs.

questions.stem: Sunlight reaching Earth is mostly visible; Earth radiates infrared. Why does that matter?
options: Greenhouse gases let visible light through but absorb infrared and re-emit it
Greenhouse gases absorb incoming visible light, so less reaches the ground
Greenhouse gases reflect outgoing infrared straight back to space
Infrared carries more energy than visible light, so it heats the air more
questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect depends on the atmosphere treating the two wavelength ranges differently: visible sunlight passes through to warm the surface, while the infrared radiated by that warm surface is absorbed by gases such as CO2, water vapour and methane and re-emitted, some of it downwards. The 'mirror reflecting infrared out to space' option sounds close but reverses the direction — energy sent to space would cool Earth, not warm it. Check the direction of the returned energy: warming requires infrared to be redirected back towards the surface.

questions.stem: Climate models include both positive (amplifying) and negative (stabilising) feedbacks. Which of these is a negative feedback?
options: Thawing permafrost lets microbes decompose old organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane
A warmer surface radiates more infrared energy, which increases losses to space and slows further warming
Melting sea ice exposes darker ocean, which absorbs more sunlight than the ice it replaced
Warmer air holds more water vapour, and water vapour is itself an effective greenhouse gas
questions.explanation: A negative feedback opposes the original change: as the surface warms it emits infrared more strongly, increasing the energy leaving Earth and partly counteracting the warming. The water vapour option is the most tempting because water vapour is often called a 'response' rather than a cause, but more vapour traps more infrared, which amplifies the warming and makes it a positive feedback. Test each loop by asking whether the end result pushes temperature further in the same direction (positive) or back the other way (negative).

questions.stem: A city replaces its diesel buses with electric buses, but the local grid is supplied mostly by coal-fired power stations. What is the best assessment of the effect on greenhouse gas emissions?
options: Emissions from the bus fleet fall to zero, because electric buses have no exhaust pipe and therefore release no greenhouse gases anywhere
Emissions rise overall, because generating and transmitting electricity always releases more carbon dioxide than burning the equivalent diesel directly
Emissions stay exactly the same, because the same quantity of energy is needed to move the buses no matter what the energy source is
Most of the emissions shift from bus exhausts to the power station, so the overall fall is much smaller than the drop in street-level emissions suggests
questions.explanation: Electrifying transport only cuts emissions as far as the electricity supply allows: with a coal-dominated grid the carbon dioxide is still released, just at the power station instead of the tailpipe. The claim that emissions fall to zero is tempting because electric vehicles genuinely have no exhaust, but that ignores where the electricity came from. When judging any electrification measure, always ask what generates the electricity — mitigation of transport emissions depends on decarbonising power generation as well.

questions.stem: Measurements show that more than 90% of the extra energy trapped by increased greenhouse gases has been absorbed by the oceans. Which consequence of this follows correctly?
options: Ocean water warms and expands, adding to sea level rise, while surface air temperatures climb more slowly than they otherwise would
The trapped energy is permanently removed from the climate system, so the atmosphere cannot warm any further while the ocean keeps absorbing
Because water is good at absorbing heat, the ocean cools the lower atmosphere back below the temperatures it had before industrialisation
The extra energy is stored as chemical energy in dissolved carbon dioxide, so the temperature of the seawater itself is essentially unchanged
questions.explanation: Energy absorbed by the ocean is stored, not destroyed: the water warms, expands slightly (thermal expansion), and this stored heat also keeps exchanging with the atmosphere, which is why surface warming lags behind the total energy imbalance. The idea that the energy is permanently removed is tempting, but the ocean is a reservoir within the climate system, not an exit from it — heat continues to move between ocean and atmosphere. Look for whether an option treats a reservoir as a one-way sink; in Earth's interacting systems, stored energy comes back into play.

questions.stem: Which gas is the main driver of recent global warming?
options: Argon
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the largest contributor. Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas, which is why abundance is a poor guide here.
questions.teaching:
Most of the atmosphere is nitrogen and oxygen, and neither absorbs infrared, so abundance is a poor guide here.

The gases that matter are the trace ones with molecules of three or more atoms, which can absorb outgoing infrared. Several qualify, and methane is actually far more potent per molecule. But the one released in by far the greatest quantity, from burning fossil fuels and clearing land, contributes the largest share of the warming — and it persists in the atmosphere for centuries. Water vapour is also a greenhouse gas, but its amount responds to temperature rather than driving it.

questions.stem: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Gases trapping heat that would otherwise leave Earth
Sunlight being reflected straight back away by clouds
The Sun growing hotter over long periods
Warm air rising from cities into the sky
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases let sunlight in but absorb the infrared Earth radiates back, keeping the surface warmer. Without any greenhouse effect Earth would be frozen — the concern is the extra warming, not the effect itself.
questions.teaching:
Two kinds of radiation are involved, and keeping them apart is the whole explanation.

Sunlight arriving at Earth is mostly visible light, and certain atmospheric gases are largely transparent to it, so it passes through and warms the ground. The warmed ground radiates energy back out, but at much longer wavelengths — infrared. Those same gases absorb infrared strongly and re-emit it in all directions, including back down. So energy enters easily and leaves with difficulty, and the surface settles at a higher temperature. Without any of this Earth would be frozen; the concern is the extra warming from adding more of those gases.

questions.stem: Where is most of Earth's carbon stored?
options: In rocks and sediments
In the atmosphere as gas
In living plants
In the ice caps
questions.explanation: By far the largest store is carbonate rock such as limestone, built up over hundreds of millions of years. The atmosphere is a tiny store by comparison, which is why moving even a little carbon into it matters so much.
questions.teaching:
Carbon moves between several reservoirs, and their sizes differ by enormous factors, which is what makes this question worth asking.

By far the largest holds carbon locked in limestone and other carbonate rock, built up from marine shells over hundreds of millions of years, plus fossil fuels formed from buried organic matter. The oceans hold a large amount dissolved. Living things and soils hold a moderate amount. The atmosphere holds the smallest share of all — which is precisely why it matters so much: moving even a small fraction from the largest store into the smallest one changes the smallest one dramatically.

questions.stem: What does 'mitigation' mean for climate change?
options: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions
Adapting to changes already underway
Measuring the rate of warming
Predicting future temperatures
questions.explanation: Mitigation tackles the cause by cutting emissions. Adaptation is the tempting pair — that means coping with change that is already coming. Most plans need both.
questions.teaching:
Responses to climate change split into two categories, and they are not alternatives — most serious plans need both.

One works on the cause, cutting the amount of greenhouse gas released or increasing how much is absorbed: renewable generation, electrifying transport, reforestation. The other works on the consequences, preparing for changes already locked in: sea walls, drought-tolerant crops, revised building codes and bushfire planning. The word in this question belongs to the first category. A useful check is whether the action would reduce future warming or merely reduce the damage from warming that is coming anyway.

questions.stem: What is a carbon sink?
options: A device that removes carbon from exhaust gases
A tax charged on carbon emissions
Something that absorbs more carbon than it releases
Something that releases more carbon than it absorbs
questions.explanation: Forests and oceans are sinks because they take up more carbon than they give back. The opposite is a carbon source, and the two options are deliberately mirror images — read the direction carefully.
questions.teaching:
Every part of the carbon cycle both takes carbon in and gives it back. What matters is the balance between the two, and the vocabulary follows from which direction wins.

Somewhere absorbing more than it releases is removing carbon from the atmosphere on balance — growing forests, the oceans, and soils accumulating organic matter all do this. Somewhere releasing more than it absorbs is doing the opposite, and gets the opposite name. The distinction is not permanent: a forest is one thing while it grows and becomes the other if it burns or is cleared, which is why land-clearing shows up in emissions accounts.

questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
options: Combustion
Decomposition
Photosynthesis
Respiration
questions.explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and build it into sugars. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all run the other way, releasing carbon dioxide back to the air.
questions.teaching:
It helps to sort the carbon-cycle processes by direction, because the options in these questions are usually two of each.

Removing it from the air: plants and algae take it in and build it into sugars using light energy. That is the only major biological process running that way. Returning it to the air: living things releasing it as they break sugars down for energy, decomposers breaking down dead material, fires and fuels burning, and volcanoes. Three of those four go the same direction, so if three options look alike and one stands apart, the odd one out is worth a close look.

questions.stem: What does burning fossil fuels release?
options: Oxygen that was locked inside the fuel
Nitrogen released from the surrounding soil
Carbon stored underground for millions of years
Carbon taken from the air within the last year or so
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels hold carbon removed from the atmosphere long ago, so burning them adds carbon the current cycle had no part in. Burning wood releases recently captured carbon instead, which is the distinction being tested.
questions.teaching:
Burning wood and burning coal both release carbon dioxide, so why is one treated so differently from the other? What separates them is where the carbon came from.

A tree took its carbon out of the atmosphere over recent decades, so burning it returns carbon that was part of the current cycle. Coal, oil and gas formed from organisms buried hundreds of millions of years ago, and that carbon has been out of circulation ever since. Burning them adds carbon the present-day cycle had no part in, which raises the atmospheric total rather than merely recirculating it. That distinction is what "fossil" is really marking.

questions.stem: What causes ocean acidification?
options: Salt concentrating as seawater evaporates
Carbon dioxide dissolving into seawater
Acid rain falling directly on the ocean
Warmer water holding less dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH. It is a separate problem from warming, and it makes shell-building harder for corals and shellfish.
questions.teaching:
This is a separate problem from warming, driven by the same gas, and it is worth understanding as its own mechanism.

The oceans absorb a large share of the carbon dioxide we release. Dissolved in seawater it forms carbonic acid, which lowers the pH — surface waters have already dropped by about 0.1, which on a logarithmic scale is a substantial change. The consequence is chemical: more acidic water makes it harder for corals, oysters and plankton to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons, and can dissolve existing ones. Acid rain is a real phenomenon but comes from sulfur and nitrogen oxides, and is not what drives this.
